    • If your instance is served under a URL path (a ROOT_URL subpath such as https://example.com/forgejo), include that prefix in the URL — e.g. https://example.com/forgejo/username/bambuddy-backup
    • If you are hosting locally without HTTPS, be sure to check the Allow insecure HTTP checkbox
    • Enter your PAT (from Step 2)
    • Click Test Connection to verify

Scoping the token to one repository

Choosing Specific in step 2 is the safest option and works from Bambuddy 1.2.6 onwards. Forgejo v15 only allows read:issue, write:issue, read:repository and write:repository on a repository-scoped token — write:repository is all a backup needs, and a token that reaches nothing else limits what a leak could cost you.

On earlier versions Test connection rejected such a token with a message about a missing read:user scope. That check no longer blocks the connection; if you hit it, update Bambuddy rather than widening the token.

Tested Versions

Bambuddy has been tested and verified against Forgejo 11.x LTS and 15.x LTS. Other versions may work but are not officially supported.

docs.title: What's Backed Up
docs.text:
Data Description Default K-profiles Per-printer pressure advance profiles (organized by serial number) On Cloud profiles Filament, printer, and process presets from Bambu Cloud and Orca Cloud, for every connected account On App settings Application configuration Off Spool inventory Filament spools, usage history, and cost tracking Off Print archives Print history metadata — each archive and each of its prints: filament, temperatures, times, costs, energy, outcome (no gcode/3MF files) Off

A cloud login is required

K-profiles need a Bambu Cloud login. Cloud profiles need at least one connected cloud account — Bambu Cloud, Orca Cloud, or both. Sign in via Profiles → Cloud Profiles or Orca Cloud Profiles. The Cloud profiles checkbox stays disabled until something is connected, and shows how many accounts are in scope.

With authentication enabled each user has their own cloud logins, and the backup collects from all of them — not just yours. Accounts appear in the repository as user-{id} directories; no email address is ever written, so the backup does not expose who signed in to what.

docs.title: Schedule Options
docs.text: Schedule Description Hourly Backup runs every hour Daily Backup runs once per day (midnight) Weekly Backup runs once per week (Sunday midnight)

docs.title: Manual Backup
docs.text: Click Backup Now to trigger an immediate backup.

docs.title: Repository Structure
docs.text:
repo/
├── backup_metadata.json
├── kprofiles/
│   └── {serial_number}/
│       ├── 0.2.json
│       ├── 0.4.json
│       └── ...
├── cloud_profiles/
│   ├── bambu/
│   │   └── {account}/          # "global", or "user-{id}" when auth is on
│   │       ├── filament.json
│   │       ├── printer.json
│   │       └── process.json
│   └── orca/
│       └── {account}/
│           ├── filament.json
│           ├── printer.json
│           └── process.json
├── settings/
│   └── app_settings.json
├── spools/
│   ├── inventory.json
│   └── usage_history.json
└── archives/
    ├── print_history.json   # One entry per archive (file)
    ├── print_runs.json      # One entry per print of it
    └── aliases.json         # Which archive was merged into which

docs.title: What cloud profiles contain
docs.text:
Only your custom presets. Bambu Cloud's bundled catalogue is skipped: it is the same hundreds of entries for every user, always re-downloadable, and cannot be recreated under your account anyway — including it would rewrite the repository on every run for nothing.

Each Bambu preset is stored with the payload needed to recreate it, not just its name. Orca profiles keep their full content, which the Orca sync API returns inline.

If an account's cloud session has expired, that account is skipped and the run says so in the log — the backup never signs anyone out on its own. For Orca Cloud the stored credentials are cleared the next time you open Orca Cloud Profiles, where you can pair again.

backup_metadata.json reports what was actually collected, per cloud and per account. If the category is enabled but nothing came back, it records false and the reason appears in the application log as a warning.

docs.title: Backup History
docs.text:
View backup history in the Backup History section:

  • Status (success, failed, skipped)
  • Trigger (manual or scheduled)
  • Files changed
  • Commit SHA (linked to GitHub)

Clear removes every entry from the history after a confirmation. The backups in the repository are not touched.

Skip Unchanged

Bambuddy only creates a commit when data has actually changed, avoiding unnecessary commits.

docs.title: Restoring from a Git Backup
docs.text: Every backup commit is a restore point. The Restore from Git button on the Git Backup card lets you pick one of those commits and pull selected categories back into Bambuddy — without touching anything you didn't select.

docs.title: How to Restore
docs.text:
1. Go to Settings > Backup & Restore
  2. On the Git Backup card, click Restore from Git
  3. Pick a Backup commit from the dropdown (the 20 most recent, newest first)
  4. Tick the categories you want under What to restore
  5. Choose whether to Overwrite existing entries (see below)
  6. Click Restore

The modal shows how many items each category holds in the commit you picked, and greys out any category that commit doesn't contain — a category you only enabled recently simply isn't in older commits. That number is what the result summary adds up to afterwards: restored plus skipped plus failed always equals it. Spool inventory counts the usage records alongside the spools, since both are restored under that category.

Restoring needs its own permission

With authentication enabled, the button only appears for users holding the github:restore permission. Configuring backups is a separate permission, so a user can be allowed to set up and run backups without being allowed to restore from them.

Each category additionally requires the permission that owns the rows it writes: settings:update for App settings, inventory:update for Spool inventory, archives:update_all for Print archives, and kprofiles:update for K-profiles. Backup is its own permission group, so without this a user holding only the Backup group could write through a restore what they cannot write through the page that owns it. Archives take archives:update_all rather than archives:create because a restore writes rows belonging to other users, and update_all is the permission that means "may write an archive that is not yours".

A restore you are not allowed to run fails with Missing required permissions: followed by every permission you are missing across the categories you ticked, so one attempt tells you everything to fix rather than one thing at a time. The check is on the server only — the modal does not grey out categories you cannot restore, so you find out when you click Restore, not before.

Granting restore to a custom role

github:restore on its own is enough to open the dialog and preview a commit, but not to write anything. A role that should be able to restore everything needs all four permissions above alongside it; one that should only put spools back needs inventory:update and nothing else. Administrators already hold every one of them.

docs.title: What Can Be Restored
docs.text:
Category Restores Notes K-profiles Pressure advance profiles, back onto the printer Needs kprofiles:update; printer must be online App settings Application configuration Needs settings:update; credential, authentication and credential-dependent keys are skipped, and so are the sign-in and mail server settings unless an administrator restores Spool inventory Spools plus their usage history Needs inventory:update; matched on tag UID Print archives Archives and their prints, metadata only Needs archives:update_all; no gcode, 3MF, or thumbnails

Cloud profiles cannot be restored

Cloud profiles are listed under What's Backed Up but are not offered as a restore category. Re-sync them from Profiles → Cloud Profiles instead.

Archives come back as metadata

A Git backup stores print history as JSON — filament, temperatures, times, costs, energy. Restoring gives you the history rows back, but the 3MF files and thumbnails are not in the repository and cannot be recovered from it. Use a local ZIP backup if you need the files.

Each print comes back with its archive

The backup holds each print of an archive: its printer, plate, start and end, duration, filament, cost, energy, failure reason and outcome. Statistics and the print log count prints, so a restore brings them back too. Each print is attached to its restored archive, and the archive then shows its latest print's outcome, as it does after a print.

A print already here is the same archive's, started at the same time on the same plate. It is skipped, or made to match the backup with Overwrite existing entries on. A print running on this instance now is never changed by a restore, nor is one that was still running when the backup was made: the one here has the figures from its end. An archive printed again since the backup is still recognised, by when it was archived and by its prints' start times, so the restore does not add a second copy of it.

Left out of the backup: the one-tap confirm link (it is a credential), photos and timelapses (their files are not in a Git backup), and wallet, cost-centre and queue links. A printer is linked again only if this instance has a printer with the same id; otherwise the print keeps the printer's name.

An archive merged into another is not restored as an archive of its own, whether the backup was made after the merge or before it. Anything that pointed at it, such as spool usage, goes to the archive it was merged into, and that archive keeps what the merge joined (notes, tags) even with overwrite on.

A print's owner comes back by username, like an archive's. A print whose user was deleted before the backup comes back with no owner, keeping the name of who started it.

Backups written before prints were included restore their archives as before, without prints.

Restored archives keep their owner

With authentication enabled, each print archive belongs to the user who made it, and users only see their own unless they have the archives:read_all permission. A restore carries that ownership across by username, so an archive lands with the same person it belonged to when the backup was taken.

The username is what makes this safe across instances. User ids are assigned in order as accounts are created, so they mean nothing on a rebuilt instance — restoring there by id would hand one person's print history to whoever happens to hold that number now, with nothing to indicate it had gone wrong. Matching on the name instead means a match is the same person, and anything else is treated as unknown rather than guessed at.

Three situations produce a newly added archive with no owner. The backup predates Bambuddy recording an owner at all; the archive genuinely had no owner on the source instance; or the name it carries does not belong to anyone here — which includes a user who still exists but has since been renamed. All three are visible only to users with archives:read_all, and the result summary says which of them happened so an administrator can reassign them.

Backups written before this change carry only the id, and those still restore: the id is used as a fallback and checked against the user table, so a stale one is dropped rather than pointing at the wrong person.

An owner the backup cannot name is never removed. If overwrite is on and the backup either predates this or names someone this instance does not have, the existing owner is left as it is — a backup that cannot tell you who owns an archive has nothing to say about it. The same applies to archives you have deleted: an older backup will not bring them back.

A print that was running when the backup was made

Its archive and that print come back as cancelled with the reason No status update received, the way Bambuddy closes a print it lost track of. It is not reported as a failed print, and no notification goes out. If this instance still has that print's archive and Overwrite existing entries is on, the archive keeps the status it has here: the print may still be running, or have ended since.

docs.title: Overwrite vs. Skip
docs.text:
The Overwrite existing entries toggle decides what happens when something in the backup already exists locally:

Toggle Behaviour Off (default) Only missing entries are added. Anything already present is left exactly as it is. On Existing entries are updated to the backed-up values as well.

Leave it off to recover something you deleted by accident. Turn it on to roll your current data back to how it looked at that commit. K-profiles are the one category the toggle doesn't reach — see the note below.

Restores never reuse the backup's IDs

Entries are matched on natural keys — a spool by its tag UID, an archive by its content hash — and re-inserted with a fresh ID if missing. A spool that was #3 when the backup was taken may come back as #5. This is deliberate: the old ID very likely belongs to an unrelated row by now. Links between restored entries (a spool and its usage history, for example) are remapped so they still line up.

Restore spools and archives together

Spool usage history records which print each entry belongs to. Restoring Spool inventory without Print archives leaves those links unresolved, so the usage entries come back without them — filament totals are still right, but the entries no longer point at a print. Restoring Print archives afterwards doesn't repair it, because the usage entries already exist by then. Tick both in the same run if you want the links kept; the result summary tells you when links were dropped.

K-profiles need the printer online

K-profiles don't live in Bambuddy's database — they live on the printer, and restoring them means writing to it over MQTT. Any printer that isn't connected is skipped, and the result says which. Reconnect it and restore again. Bambuddy resolves each profile's current slot on the printer before writing, so profiles you have edited since the backup are still updated correctly. If the printer rejects a batch, those profiles are counted as failed and the result gives the printer's own reason. A printer that doesn't answer at all still counts as restored — older firmware never answers — so verify the values on the printer or in Profiles → K-Profiles afterwards.

Overwrite existing entries doesn't apply to K-profiles. Writing a slot on the printer is always a replacement — there is no "add only if missing" for a value the printer already holds — so a K-profile restore updates the matching slot whichever way you set the toggle, replacing the calibration currently on the printer. The restore screen says so beside the category as soon as you tick it, and the result summary repeats it.

Credentials are never backed up or restored

Tokens, secrets, passwords, access codes, API keys, and passphrases are written to the backup as ******** (or left empty if they were never set), never as the value, and are skipped on restore. A URL setting with a login in it, such as http://user:password@host, is left out of the backup. In cloud profiles, a printer preset's connection credentials (the printer's access code or the print host's API key, user and password) are written as ******** too, and a login in any URL in the preset is masked. Re-enter them by hand if you're rebuilding an instance. Settings Bambuddy no longer uses, left in the database by earlier versions, are not backed up at all.

A credential stored on this instance is never sent somewhere the backup names: if the backup would change where it goes (the MQTT broker, port or TLS setting, the SMTP server, port or security mode, the Home Assistant URL, the Obico ML URL or the Manyfold URL), those settings are left as they are and the restore says so. Change them in Settings and enter the credential again. A Home Assistant token set through the HA_TOKEN environment variable is the exception and follows the URL.

Backups made by earlier versions did contain these values, and they stay in your backup repository's history. If you used Git backup before, change those passwords and tokens.

Each restored value is checked like an edit in Settings

A restore writes a setting only if Settings would accept the same value when you edit it: a Home Assistant, Obico, slicer, Manyfold or Spoolman URL must pass the same address checks, the Docker Compose directory may hold only path characters, and JSON and numeric settings must be well-formed and in range. A value that fails is skipped and named in the result. So is anything that is not a setting you edit here: account sessions for Bambu Cloud and Orca Cloud, the automatic purge schedules for archives and the library trash (set them again under their own pages; they need the purge permission), runtime state, and keys this version does not know. Bambuddy's own internal flags are skipped without a mention. Each user's email sign-in codes are never changed by a restore.

A restore also never changes where Bambuddy sends things: the External URL (password reset and welcome links are built from it), the mail server, the local backup folder, the MQTT broker, and the Home Assistant, Obico, slicer, Spoolman and Manyfold addresses. A value in the backup that differs from this instance's is left as it is here and named in the result, even if nothing is set here yet. On a fresh instance, enter these addresses again in Settings.

Authentication settings are never restored either

Four settings are refused even with Overwrite existing entries on: whether authentication is enabled, Advanced Authentication, local login, and whether first-time setup has completed. Restoring those would change who can reach Bambuddy rather than how it behaves — a backup taken before you turned authentication on would switch it back off, and the checks that stop you disabling local login without a working OIDC provider don't run on a restore.

The whole LDAP configuration is refused with them, not just the bind password: the server URL, search base, user filter, security mode, group mapping, auto-provision and default group. Together those name which directory server decides who you are, and Bambuddy reads them on every login — so restoring them from a file would let the file choose the directory that authenticates your users.

Change all of these in Settings → Authentication instead. Rebuilding an instance means setting LDAP up again by hand; that is deliberate.

A switch is left off when its credential can't come with it

Because credentials are never restored, turning a switch on without one would leave the integration in a worse state than either the backup or your current instance. Four pairs are treated as travelling together:

Switch Credential it needs Prometheus metrics Prometheus token MQTT relay MQTT password Home Assistant Home Assistant token Virtual printer Virtual printer access code

A switch is left off when the backup has it on and this instance has no usable credential of its own. For the MQTT relay, Home Assistant and the virtual printer there is one further condition: the backup must have carried a non-empty credential too. An anonymous MQTT broker is a perfectly valid setup, so a backup describing one restores as normal — the restore isn't leaving you with anything weaker than what was backed up. Nor is anything already switched on locally affected, for the same reason.

LDAP is not in this table. It used to be, paired with its bind password, but an anonymous bind is a valid setup too — which meant a backup that simply left the password out had its LDAP switch restored. That is fine for an integration and wrong for a login source, so LDAP is refused outright instead (see above) rather than judged on whether it would still work.

Prometheus is the exception, deliberately. /api/v1/metrics is unauthenticated whenever no token is set, so restoring that switch onto an instance with no token publishes your metrics to anyone who can reach the port. The token is optional, which means the likeliest backup to do that is one taken on an instance that had metrics switched on and never set a token — so for Prometheus the switch is left off whenever this instance has no token, whether or not the backup carried one.

Fill the credential in under the relevant settings section, then turn the switch on yourself.

The result summary reports all three groups in its notes.

docs.title: After Restoring
docs.text:
The result summary lists restored / skipped / failed counts per category, plus any notes explaining a skip. Those three add up to the item count the preview showed for that category.

A failed restore can still have applied part of itself

Categories are written one at a time and each is committed as it finishes, so a restore that fails part-way through leaves the categories that already completed in place rather than undoing them. The summary reports those rather than claiming nothing was restored, so what it lists is what is actually on disk. Re-running the restore is safe — with overwrite off, anything already restored is recognised and skipped.

If App settings was one of the restored categories, Bambuddy reloads the page when you close the modal. Most restored settings appear immediately, but the ones the interface applies at startup, such as whether authentication is on, won't until it reloads. The restored SpoolBuddy display language applies to the SpoolBuddy displays only; each browser keeps its own interface language, chosen in the account menu.

If any MQTT settings were restored, Bambuddy reconnects the MQTT relay to the restored broker immediately, so you don't need to restart for those to take effect. The MQTT password isn't in the backup, so a broker that needs a different one won't connect until you re-enter it — the result summary says when the relay couldn't reconnect.

Restores are recorded in Backup History with a restore trigger, alongside your backup runs.

An older backup can bring back archives that hold the same file more than once (merged since, or from before Bambuddy kept one archive per file). After a restore that included archives, the result says how many groups of such duplicates there are and offers Merge duplicates…. Nothing is merged unless you do it; see Merging duplicates.

docs.title: Restore API Endpoints
Scheduled Local Backups
docs.text: Automate local backups on a recurring schedule so you never forget to protect your data.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The Scheduled Backups card in Settings > Backup lets you configure automatic local backups that run in the background. Each backup produces the same complete ZIP file as a manual backup (database + all data directories), stored on disk where you can easily copy them to a NAS or external drive.

Works with both SQLite and PostgreSQL installations.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Setting Options Default Enable On / Off Off Frequency Hourly, Daily, Weekly Daily Time of day Time picker (for Daily and Weekly) 00:00 Retention count 1--100 5 Output path Any local or network path DATA_DIR/backups/

Retention

When a new backup completes, Bambuddy automatically deletes the oldest backups beyond the retention count. For example, with retention set to 5, only the 5 most recent backups are kept.

Timezone

The time-of-day picker is interpreted in the container's local timezone, read from the TZ environment variable. The resolved zone name (e.g. Europe/Berlin) is shown next to the picker. If TZ is not set, times are interpreted as UTC. Set TZ in docker-compose.yml (e.g. TZ=Europe/Berlin) to match your local time.

docs.title: Managing Backups
docs.text:
Each backup in the list supports three actions:

  • Download -- download the ZIP file to your browser
  • Restore -- restore directly from the backup (same as manual restore)
  • Delete -- remove the backup file from disk

Click Run Now to trigger an immediate backup outside the schedule.

docs.title: Docker Setup
docs.text:
Docker users should mount the backup output directory as a volume so backups are persisted outside the container. Add a bind mount to your docker-compose.yml:

services:
  bambuddy:
    image: ghcr.io/maziggy/bambuddy:latest
    container_name: bambuddy
    network_mode: host
    volumes:
      - bambuddy_data:/app/data
      - bambuddy_logs:/app/logs
      - /path/to/nas/bambuddy-backups:/app/data/backups  # Scheduled backup output
    environment:
      - TZ=Europe/Berlin
    restart: unless-stopped

volumes:
  bambuddy_data:
  bambuddy_logs:

Or with docker run:

docker run -d \
  --network host \
  -v bambuddy_data:/app/data \
  -v bambuddy_logs:/app/logs \
  -v /path/to/nas/bambuddy-backups:/app/data/backups \
  -e TZ=Europe/Berlin \
  --name bambuddy \
  --restart unless-stopped \
  ghcr.io/maziggy/bambuddy:latest

NAS or Network Share

Point the bind mount at a NAS share, Samba mount, or NFS path for automatic off-site backups without any extra scripts.

An output path that isn't mounted is worse than one that fails

If the Output path points somewhere that is not bind-mounted from the host, the backups still succeed -- they land in the container's own writable layer and are lost the next time the container is recreated (compose up after an image update, for example). Bambuddy detects this and warns on the backup card, but the rule is simple: whatever you set as the output path must appear in volumes:.

docs.title: Non-Docker Setup
docs.text:
For bare-metal or virtual machine installs, set the Output path in the UI to any directory your Bambuddy process can write to -- a local folder, a mounted network drive, or an external USB drive.

systemd: a NAS share needs to be allowed explicitly

Bambuddy's systemd unit runs with ProtectSystem=strict. That makes every directory outside the install, data and log directories read-only for the service -- including a NAS share you mounted yourself and can write to from your own shell. Backups there fail with [Errno 30] Read-only file system, which looks like a permission problem but is not one (errno 30 is EROFS; a permission problem is errno 13).

Add the path to the unit's writable list with a drop-in, which survives reinstalls and upgrades:

sudo systemctl edit bambuddy

[Service]
ReadWritePaths=/mnt/nasbackup

sudo systemctl restart bambuddy

Confirm it took with systemctl show bambuddy -p ReadWritePaths.

Bambuddy checks the output directory when you save it and tells you if it cannot write there, so you should not have to work this out from a failed backup at 03:00. Installing over an existing setup keeps any paths you added -- the installer backs the old unit up and carries them forward.

docs.title: API Endpoints
docs.text:
For automation or monitoring, the scheduled backup system exposes a REST API:

Method Endpoint Description GET /local-backup/status Current schedule config and next run time GET /local-backup/path-check Check the output directory is writable (writes and removes a probe file) POST /local-backup/run Trigger an immediate backup GET /local-backup/backups List all backup files GET /local-backup/backups/{filename}/download Download a backup file POST /local-backup/backups/{filename}/restore Restore from a backup file DELETE /local-backup/backups/{filename} Delete a backup file

docs.title: Manual Backup
docs.text:
1. Go to Settings > Backup & Restore
  2. Click Download Backup
  3. Wait for backup to complete (progress indicator shown)
  4. ZIP file downloads automatically

Don't Navigate Away

During backup/restore, stay on the page. The UI blocks navigation to prevent data corruption.

docs.title: Backup Contents
docs.text:
The backup is a complete ZIP file containing:

Data Included Database (all tables) Print archives (3MF files) Archive thumbnails Timelapse videos Library files Library thumbnails Project files Printer icons Plate calibration data Virtual printer uploads

Complete by Definition

The new backup system copies the entire database file and all data directories. No data can be missed because everything is included automatically.

docs.title: Format
docs.text:
Backup files are ZIP archives:

bambuddy-backup-20260201-143022.zip

docs.title: ZIP Structure
docs.text:
bambuddy-backup-YYYYMMDD-HHMMSS.zip
├── manifest.json            # Which Bambuddy version made this backup
├── bambuddy.db              # Database (portable SQLite format, works on both SQLite and PostgreSQL installs)
├── archive/                 # All archive data
│   ├── <archive_id>/        # Individual archive folders
│   │   ├── *.3mf            # Archived print files
│   │   ├── thumbnail.png    # Thumbnails
│   │   ├── timelapse.mp4    # Timelapses
│   │   ├── source.3mf       # Original source 3MF
│   │   ├── *.f3d            # Fusion 360 files
│   │   └── photos/*.jpg     # Photo attachments
│   └── library/             # File Manager
│       ├── files/           # Uploaded files
│       ├── thumbnails/      # Generated thumbnails
│       └── photos/<id>/     # Photos attached to library files
├── virtual_printer/         # Pending uploads
├── projects/                # Project files
├── icons/                   # Custom printer icons
└── plate_calibration/       # Plate detection references

docs.title: File Size
docs.text:
Typical sizes depend on your archive content:

  • Small archive (100 prints, no timelapses): ~100-500 MB
  • Medium archive (500 prints, some timelapses): ~1-5 GB
  • Large archive (1000+ prints, full timelapses): ~10+ GB

Large Backups

If you have many timelapse videos, backups can be large. Consider periodic cleanup of old timelapses.

docs.title: Full Restore
docs.text:
Restore everything from a backup ZIP:

  1. Go to Settings > Backup & Restore
  2. Click Restore Backup
  3. Select your backup ZIP file
  4. Wait for restore to complete (progress indicator shown)
  5. Restart Bambuddy when prompted

Full Restore Overwrites

A full restore replaces all current data including the database and all files. Create a backup first!

Restart Required

After restore, you must restart Bambuddy for changes to take effect. The database connection is replaced during restore.

If the restored database holds archives of the same file more than once, the Archives page offers to merge them (see Merging duplicates). Nothing is merged unless you do it.

docs.title: Portable Backups
docs.text:
Backups are fully portable between installations:

  • Different servers: Move from one machine to another
  • Different paths: Works even if data directory changed
  • Different Docker volumes: Migrate between container setups
  • Different database backends: Restore a SQLite backup into a PostgreSQL install (and vice versa)

The backup system always exports data in portable SQLite format, regardless of which database backend you use. When restoring into PostgreSQL, Bambuddy automatically converts data types (booleans, datetimes) and handles foreign key constraints.

docs.title: Backups and versions
docs.text:
A backup carries the database of the version that made it, and manifest.json records which version that was. Restoring into a different version is normal and supported in both directions: a newer Bambuddy migrates an older backup forward after the restore, and a column a newer backup has but an older version does not know about is ignored.

The one case that cannot work is a column the version you are restoring into requires and the backup has no value for. On a PostgreSQL install that is checked before the restore starts, and an incompatible backup is refused with a message naming the columns and both version numbers — nothing is changed, so your current data is still there. If you see it, restore the backup on the version that made it, or upgrade this install to that version first.

Keep the versions together

The simplest way to never meet this is to upgrade before restoring: restore a backup into the same version or a newer one, never into an older one. Downgrading an install and restoring yesterday's backup into it is the combination that gets caught.

docs.title: Manual Database Access
docs.text: SQLite (Default) PostgreSQL

docs.title: Location
docs.text:
The database is stored at:

/path/to/bambuddy/bambuddy.db

docs.title: Direct Backup
docs.text:
Copy the database file directly:

cp bambuddy.db bambuddy_backup_$(date +%Y%m%d).db

Stop Bambuddy First

Stop Bambuddy before copying to ensure consistency.

docs.title: SQLite Tools
docs.text:
Use SQLite tools for advanced operations:

```bash

docs.title: Dump to SQL
docs.text: sqlite3 bambuddy.db .dump > backup.sql

docs.title: Connection
docs.text:
Connect to your PostgreSQL database using the same DATABASE_URL from your configuration:

psql "postgresql://user:pass@host:5432/bambuddy"

docs.title: Direct Backup
docs.text: pg_dump -Fc "postgresql://user:pass@host:5432/bambuddy" > bambuddy_backup_$(date +%Y%m%d).dump

docs.title: Restore
docs.text:
pg_restore --clean --if-exists -d "postgresql://user:pass@host:5432/bambuddy" bambuddy_backup.dump

Bambuddy's Built-in Backup is Easier

The Settings > Backup page creates portable backups that work across both SQLite and PostgreSQL. Use manual pg_dump only if you need PostgreSQL-specific features like point-in-time recovery.

docs.title: Restore from SQL
docs.text: sqlite3 new.db < backup.sql ```

docs.title: Downloading Archives
docs.text: 3MF files aren't in database backups. Download separately:

docs.title: Individual Download
docs.text:
1. Open an archive
  2. Click Download 3MF

docs.title: Bulk Export
docs.text:
1. Go to Archives
  2. Click Export
  3. Select Include 3MF files
  4. Download the archive

docs.title: Lost Database
docs.text:
If database is corrupted or deleted:

  1. Stop Bambuddy
  2. Remove corrupted bambuddy.db
  3. Start Bambuddy (creates fresh database)
  4. Go to Settings > Backup
  5. Restore from your backup

docs.title: New Installation
docs.text:
Moving to a new server:

  1. Install Bambuddy on new server
  2. Copy backup file to new server
  3. Go to Settings > Backup
  4. Full restore from backup

docs.title: Data Migration
docs.text:
Moving between versions:

  1. Create backup on old version
  2. Upgrade Bambuddy
  3. If needed, restore from backup

docs.title: Recommended Backup Frequency
docs.text: Frequency Good For Daily Active printing (use Scheduled Local Backups) Weekly Regular use Monthly Light use

docs.title: Storage
docs.text:
• Keep backups off the Bambuddy server
  • Use cloud storage (Dropbox, Google Drive, etc.)
  • Keep multiple versions

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
• Periodically test restoring
  • Verify backup integrity
  • Document your backup process

docs.title: Tips
docs.text:
Before Major Changes

Always backup before upgrading or making big configuration changes.

Off-Site Storage

Store at least one backup off-site (cloud or another location).

Regular Testing

Test your restore process periodically to ensure backups work.

Version in Filename

Include date and version in backup filenames for easy identification.

3MF Backup

For complete backup, also download your 3MF files separately.

docs.title: Billing & Cost Centers
docs.text:
Bambuddy has always been able to tell you what a print cost. Billing tells you whose budget it came out of — and, when you want it, stops a print that would go over.

It is aimed at installs where somebody has to be billed: a lab charging research groups, a makerspace with member accounts, a department splitting machine time between projects. It is entirely optional, off by default, and nothing about an existing install changes until you turn it on.

docs.title: What it does
docs.text:
• Cost centers — a budget somebody can print against: a team, a course, a customer, a grant. Every user also gets a private one automatically.
  • Budgets — an optional total or monthly limit per cost center. A center with no budget is explicitly unlimited, not blocked.
  • Reservations — a queued print's cost is held against the budget while it waits, so ten queued jobs cannot each pass a check that only the last would fail.
  • A ledger — every charge, deposit, withdrawal and adjustment, on one page, with the cost center it belongs to.
  • Server-side costing — the estimate that budgets are enforced against is computed by Bambuddy, not sent by the browser.
  • Proportional charging — a print that fails half way is charged for the filament it actually used.
  • A charging policy — a charge is the filament by default; you choose whether completed and failed prints also pay their energy and printer wear, and how a failed print's filament is charged.

docs.title: Turning it on
docs.text:
Settings → General → Cost Tracking

Setting Default Range What it does Billing enabled Off — Turns the whole feature on. While off, no cost center is required, no budget is checked, and the Finance page is not in the sidebar. Printer kill switch Off — Stops prints that start without going through Bambuddy. Separate switch — see Printer kill switch below, and read it before enabling. Budget reset day 1 1–31 Day of the month a monthly budget window restarts. Clamped on short months, so 31 means the last day of February. Budget reset timezone UTC IANA name The timezone that reset day is measured in, e.g. Europe/Berlin. Teams spread across timezones otherwise disagree about which month a print landed in.

The Finance page appears when billing does

The Finance entry sits between Statistics and Settings in the sidebar, and only while billing is enabled. If you have rearranged your sidebar, it appears wherever you put it.

docs.title: Cost centers
docs.text:
A cost center is created and staffed on the Finance page by an administrator.

Private cost centers are created automatically, one per user, and are the reason a single-user install works the moment billing is switched on. They belong to their owner: nobody else can print against them, and they cannot be renamed, deactivated or deleted. An administrator can set their budget; a budget of 0 refuses every print with an estimated cost.

Shared cost centers are created by an administrator, who then adds members. Each member carries a can print flag, so somebody can be given visibility of a budget without being able to spend it.

Each center can carry a total budget (a fixed pot) or a monthly budget (refreshed on the reset day above). A center with neither is shown as Unlimited — printing against it is never blocked, and its spending is still recorded.

A cost center in use cannot be deleted

Deletion is refused while any transaction or active reservation references the center, because removing it would rewrite the history of everyone who ever printed against it. Deactivate it instead — an inactive center cannot be selected for new prints, and its ledger stays intact.

docs.title: Balances and budgets are not the same thing
docs.text:
This is the one thing worth reading twice.

What it means Does it stop a print? Balance What a user has spent, deposited and been adjusted by No Cost center budget The limit set on the center a print is billed to Yes

A balance is a record, not a credit limit. A user sitting at a negative balance can still print; only the budget on the selected cost center can refuse a job. If you want spending to stop somewhere, set a budget there.

A personal balance counts charges with no cost center, plus charges to the user's own private center. A print billed to a shared center does not move the personal balance — it belongs to the team that paid for it.

docs.title: What happens when you print
docs.text:
1. Pick a cost center. With billing on, the print dialog shows an estimated cost and a cost center picker. If you have no active center you are allowed to print against, the dialog says so and the print is refused — ask an administrator for print access on one.
  2. The budget is checked against what the center has already spent in the current window, plus anything reserved for prints that have not run yet. If the job does not fit, it is refused with the amounts in the message.
  3. A reservation is taken when the item is queued, and released if the print never happens.
  4. The charge is written when the print ends, from the archive's measured cost rather than the estimate.

The estimate and the charge are different numbers

The estimate is what the file and your printer's rates predict; the charge is what the print actually consumed. They will rarely be identical, and the charge is the one that lands in the ledger. The figure in the dialog is a display hint only — budget enforcement uses Bambuddy's own calculation, so editing it in the browser cannot buy a bigger budget.

Every print is charged at the spools it prints with. When a print starts, Bambuddy estimates its cost: its plate's planned filament at the spools mapped for it, which is the mapping chosen in the print dialog or stored on the queue item, or the loaded trays whose colours match. The print is charged from that start estimate. A reprint is priced the same way, so printing an archive again on a spool that cost more, or after the spool's price changed, is charged at the new price. A first print of one plate of a multi-plate file is charged from that plate's own figure as well, not from the whole file's cost scaled to the plate's share.

The charge is the estimate made at the start, not the cost measured at the end. The Print Log shows each print's measured cost, which can differ from what was charged; in Spoolman mode that measured cost may not be priced from the spool at all. A completed print with no measured cost, a first print included, is logged at what it was charged. The archive card keeps showing its first print's cost.

If a print ends before its start estimate was worked out (it failed within seconds, or Bambuddy restarted while it printed), it is priced when it ends, from the spools in its trays at that moment.

A print Bambuddy could not price from its spools (no mapping, no spool in the mapped trays, or the file is gone) is charged from the archive's cost. The budget a queued reprint reserves is priced like its charge when the queue item has a spool mapping, and is the archive's cost without one. It is worked out when the job is queued and again when it is sent to the printer. By then the queue has mapped the job's filaments to the printer's slots, so a job queued without a mapping is priced at its spools there. The charge can still differ from the reservation if a spool or its price changes before the print starts. In Spoolman mode the reservation finds a spool the way the charge does: by its RFID tag first, then by its slot assignment in Bambuddy.

A spool of the built-in inventory priced 0 counts as free. A print only on such spools is charged nothing and reserves nothing, and it is not refused for having no estimated cost. This applies to the built-in inventory only: in Spoolman a price of 0 means the spool has no price, and its filament is charged at the default filament cost.

A built-in spool with no price at all is not a free one. Its filament is charged at the default filament cost. If that is set to 0, such a spool does not price the print: a print only on spools without a price is charged from the archive's cost, and reserves that, not 0.

With billing off, prints and queued jobs are not priced for a charge, and queueing a job does not ask Spoolman for prices.

Aborted prints are charged proportionally. A job stopped part way is billed for the filament it consumed, not for the whole job.

A job is never charged twice. Each dispatch carries its own billing identity, so a reprint of the same file is a new charge, a restart mid-print does not produce a second one, and a charge that was deleted by an administrator does not come back on the next reprint.

A print is billed to the user who queued it. A reprint of someone else's archive is charged under the person who sent it, not the archive's owner.

Deleting a user does not cancel the cost of a print still running. It is charged to its cost center when it ends, including the user's own private center (which stays after them), and shows No user in the ledger, as do prints that never had a user (login turned off). Deleting the user together with their items releases the budget their queued prints still held; a print of theirs that is still running is kept until it ends, without a user, and billed the same way.

A charge that fails is loud. If a charge cannot be written, Bambuddy reports it in the interface and through any notification provider subscribed to the Billing charge failed event, rather than quietly not billing.

docs.title: Print charges: energy, wear and failed prints
docs.text:
By default a charge covers the filament: all of it for a completed print, the share it used for a print that failed or was cancelled. Bambuddy also works out two more costs for every print: its energy, measured by the printer's smart plug, and its printer wear, the print's duration at the printer's wear cost per printing hour. The charging policy decides which of these a print pays.

Settings → General → Cost Tracking → Print Charges, shown while billing is enabled:

Setting Default What it does Completed prints Energy Cost Off Adds the print's energy cost. Needs a smart plug with energy monitoring on the printer. Wear Cost Off Adds the print's wear cost. Needs a wear cost per printing hour on the printer; a printer without one adds nothing. Failed and cancelled prints Filament charge Amount used Amount used charges the filament in proportion to what the print consumed. Full print charges it as if the print had completed. Not charged charges no filament. Energy Cost Off Adds the energy the print used before it stopped. Wear Cost Off Adds the wear for the time the print ran.

A completed print always pays its filament. With the defaults, charges are exactly as before.

Energy and wear do not depend on the filament

Energy Cost and Wear Cost are charged whenever they are switched on for how the print ended, also when its filament costs nothing: a print on free spools still used the printer and the power.

The charge stays one ledger entry, and its description lists what it is made of:

Print charge: Benchy (filament 1.20 + energy 0.08 + wear 0.25)
Print charge: Benchy (filament 0.60 + energy 0.08) [failed: 50.0% filament (50.0g/100.0g)]
Print charge: Benchy (filament 1.20; filament charged in full) [failed: full filament]
Print charge: Benchy (energy 0.08 + wear 0.25; filament not charged) [failed: filament not charged]

The part in square brackets is how a print that did not finish ended and what was charged for its filament. The Finance page shows it as a badge on the entry instead of in the description.

  • Energy and wear are the print's actual values, also for a print that did not finish: what the plug measured and how long the printer ran.
  • A print that pays no filament still pays its energy and wear, if those are switched on for how it ended. That covers a completed print with no filament cost (free spools, an archive with no filament data), a failed print under Not charged, and a failed print Bambuddy has no filament data for. Its description then lists only what was charged: Print charge: Benchy (energy 0.08 + wear 0.25). With nothing left to charge, no entry is written and the print's reservation is released.
  • Energy is read a few seconds after the print ends. A print that pays energy, and whose plug was read at its start, is charged once the plug has been read again, instead of at the moment it ends. Every other print is charged when it ends, as before.
  • If the energy cannot be read (no plug, the plug is unreachable, or its counter was reset during the print), the print is charged without it and the description says so: (filament 1.20 + wear 0.25; energy not available).
  • Energy is charged only from one plug. The energy is the difference between the plug's counter at the start and at the end of the print. If the plug read at the start does not answer at the end and another plug of the printer does, the two readings are from different counters, and the print is charged with energy not available.
  • A print that ended while its printer was offline pays no energy. That is any print whose end Bambuddy did not see: the printer was disconnected, or Bambuddy was not running. Its end is noticed at the reconnect, and the plug's reading then also holds everything since the print really ended (idle draw, other prints). Such a print is charged when it is noticed, with energy not available. Its wear is charged when Bambuddy can still work out when the print ended, for that duration, and is nothing otherwise.
  • The policy that counts is the one in force when the print ends. A charge waiting for its energy is not changed by a setting changed meanwhile.
  • A restart does not lose the charge. A charge that was waiting for its energy when Bambuddy stopped is written at the next start, with the energy if it had been saved, without it otherwise. If that fails, the Billing charge failed alert is sent, once, and the charge is tried again at each following start. Whatever removes the print's log entry or its archive while its charge is waiting writes the charge first: clearing the print log or deleting an entry, deleting or purging the archive, deleting its printer with its archives, deleting its user with their items, and merging archives. A waiting charge whose archive is gone all the same cannot be written: the Billing charge failed alert is sent and the print's reservation is released.
  • Budgets cover the filament only. The budget check and the reservation taken for a queued print use the filament estimate, without energy or wear. With those switched on, a center can end up slightly over its budget.
  • The Print Log's cost stays the filament. With Energy Cost or Wear Cost on, the Print Log still shows a print's filament cost as its cost, and its energy and wear in their own fields. The charge is the three together: the filament, priced at the spools the print prints with, plus its energy and wear. So a completed print with no measured cost is logged at the filament part of its charge, not at the whole charge.
  • The policy applies to every cost center.

docs.title: The Finance page
docs.text:
Users see their own balance and ledger. Administrators additionally get an Admin view covering every user and cost center:

  • Cost centers — create, rename, deactivate, set total or monthly budgets, add and remove members, and set who may print
  • Transactions — filter the whole ledger by user, cost center and type; edit or delete an entry; move a transaction back to a personal account
  • Deposits and withdrawals — credit or debit a user's account
  • Manual print charge — record a job that happened outside Bambuddy

Amounts use the currency configured in Settings → General.

docs.title: Permissions
docs.text:
Permission Grants cost_centers:read_own See your own balance, ledger and the cost centers you may print against cost_centers:read_all See every user's balance and the full ledger cost_centers:modify Edit cost centers, budgets, members and transactions cost_centers:create Create new cost centers

The default Administrators group holds all four. Operators hold cost_centers:read_own, so they can see their own spending and print against the centers they belong to. Grant the rest to whoever does your accounting.

docs.title: API keys
docs.text: With billing on, a job queued through an API key needs a cost_center_id like any other. A key with Manage Queue finds the ones it may use at GET /api/v1/finance/cost-centers/mine. That endpoint returns the cost centers of the key's owner, and a key can charge only those, or any center if its owner is an administrator. A key created before keys had owners has none, and needs to be recreated to queue with billing on. Balances, the ledger and cost-center administration stay closed to API keys.

docs.title: Printer kill switch
docs.text:
Settings → General → Cost Tracking → Printer kill switch. Off by default, and separate from billing itself.

An install that bills its users can be bypassed by sending a job straight to the printer from Bambu Studio or Handy — that print is not queued, not costed and not billed. With the kill switch on, Bambuddy stops such a print as soon as it sees it, raises an alert in the interface, and sends the configured print-stopped notification. Its archive is marked cancelled, with the reason Stopped by the printer kill switch, so it does not count as a failed print.

This stops prints, and a stopped print is not recoverable

Enable it only where prints genuinely must not start outside Bambuddy. It acts on any print it can show did not come from Bambuddy, including one started deliberately by an administrator at the machine. The printer's built-in calibration (started on the printer's screen or from the slicer's device page) is left alone; a calibration print sent from Bambu Studio, such as the pressure-advance line, is a print like any other and is stopped. On an A1, A1 Mini, P1 or A2L the built-in calibration reports itself under a plain file name that any file could be given, so it is stopped too: switch the kill switch off while calibrating those printers.

It is deliberately cautious about what it can prove. When ownership of a running print cannot be established — during the moments after a Bambuddy restart, or while a job Bambuddy dispatched is still being recorded — it does nothing and logs that it deferred. Stopping a print is irreversible; declining to act costs a log line.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• Balances do not gate printing — only cost center budgets do. See above.
  • Monthly budgets reset, they do not roll over. Unspent budget from last month is not added to this month's.
  • The kill switch works on prints it observes, so it acts after the printer has started rather than preventing the start.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
"No active cost center is available for printing" — you are not a member of any active cost center with print rights. An administrator can add you on the Finance page, or check that the center has not been deactivated.

A print was refused for budget — the message carries the requested amount and what remains. Remember that queued prints hold reservations: cancelling a queued job releases its reservation immediately.

The Finance page is missing from the sidebar — billing is off, or your account lacks cost_centers:read_own.

A balance looks wrong after an administrator edited a transaction — balances are recomputed from the ledger, so the ledger is the source of truth. If a figure still looks wrong, an administrator can rebuild the balance ledger from the Finance page.

docs.title: Bug Report
docs.text: Submit bug reports directly from the Bambuddy UI without leaving the application.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The in-app bug report feature provides a quick way to report issues:

  • One-click access — Floating bug button in the bottom-right corner on wide screens, or in the top bar on narrower ones
  • Screenshot support — Upload, paste from clipboard, or drag & drop images
  • Interactive debug capture — Start logging, reproduce the issue at your own pace, stop, review and submit
  • Privacy-first — All sensitive data is sanitized before submission
  • GitHub integration — Reports create GitHub issues automatically

docs.title: Setup-problem check
docs.text:
When you open the bug report form, Bambuddy quietly runs a Connection Diagnostic against your printers. If a printer has a connection problem — a blocked port, LAN Developer Mode turned off, Docker bridge networking, wrong access code — the detected issue and its fix are shown right in the form.

Most bug reports turn out to be setup issues, so it's worth reading this panel first: fixing the highlighted problem often resolves things without a report. You can still submit a report regardless.

docs.title: Submitting a Report
docs.text:
1. Click the red bug icon. Where it sits depends on your window width:

    Wide window (1144px and up)Narrow window, tablet, or phone

    Floating red button in the bottom-right corner of any page.

    Red bug icon in the top bar, at the right-hand end beside the Bambuddy logo — the same bar that holds the menu button.

    Why it moves

    The bottom-right corner is where most on-screen controls live: the scroll-to-top button, the floating camera window, page action bars, and the buttons on file and archive cards. On a narrow screen a fixed button pinned to that corner sits on top of whichever of them happens to be underneath. Once the sidebar collapses into a menu button, the bug icon moves into that top bar so the corner stays clear. Nothing is hidden and the report form is identical either way.

  2. Describe the issue — What went wrong? Steps to reproduce?

  3. Add a screenshot (optional) — Upload a file, paste from clipboard (Ctrl+V), or drag & drop an image onto the upload area. Images are automatically compressed to JPEG.
  4. Add your email (optional) — If provided, your email will be included in a collapsed section of the GitHub issue so the maintainer can follow up. Bambuddy itself does not keep it.
  5. Click Start Debug Logging

docs.title: Debug Log Capture
docs.text:
After clicking Start Debug Logging, a 3-step guided flow begins:

  1. Debug logging enabled — Bambuddy enables debug-level logging and queries all connected printers for fresh status data
  2. Reproduce the issue now — An elapsed timer counts up while you reproduce the bug at your own pace. Take as long as you need (auto-stops after 5 minutes).
  3. Stop logging and review the report — Click Stop Logging when you're done reproducing

Stopping turns debug logging back off and collects the logs, but sends nothing yet. The panel then says what submitting will do and how many log lines were collected:

  • Submit posts the report as a public issue on GitHub, with your description, screenshot, email (in a collapsed section), system info and the sanitized logs.
  • Discard throws the report away. Nothing is sent.

The 5-minute auto-stop ends on the same review, so a capture left running is never filed on its own. Closing the panel during the review keeps it; a page reload loses it.

Close the panel to get at the thing you're reproducing

The panel sits over part of the page, which is awkward when the bug you're reproducing is behind it. Close it — recording keeps going. The bug button turns amber while a capture is running, and clicking it puts you back on step 2 with your description and the timer intact. A page reload is fine too. Only Stop Logging (or the 5-minute auto-stop) ends the capture and turns debug logging back off.

docs.title: Data Privacy
docs.text: The bug report includes a detailed, expandable privacy notice explaining exactly what data is collected.

docs.title: Included in the report
docs.text:
• App version, OS, architecture, Python version
  • Database statistics (counts only)
  • Printer models, nozzle counts, firmware versions
  • Connectivity status
  • Integration status (Spoolman, MQTT, Home Assistant)
  • Non-sensitive settings
  • Network interface count
  • Docker details
  • Dependency versions
  • Sanitized application logs (last 200 lines)

docs.title: Never included
docs.text:
• Printer names or serial numbers
  • Access codes or passwords
  • IP addresses
  • Email addresses (except your own, if you provide it)
  • API keys or tokens
  • Webhook URLs
  • Hostnames or usernames
  • LDAP Distinguished Names (a DN's CN is the user's real name)

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
Bug reports are submitted through a secure relay service on bambuddy.cool. This relay:

  • Holds the GitHub API token server-side (never shipped in the application)
  • Uploads screenshots and log files to GitHub
  • Creates issues with appropriate labels
  • Rate-limited to prevent abuse (5 reports per hour)

Your Bambuddy instance never needs a GitHub token — the relay handles all GitHub communication.

docs.title: Camera Streaming
docs.text: Monitor your prints visually with live camera streaming directly from your Bambu Lab printer.

docs.title: Live Streaming
docs.text: Bambuddy provides MJPEG video streaming from your printer's built-in camera, or from an external network camera.

docs.title: External Cameras
docs.text: Connect external network cameras to replace the built-in printer camera. Useful for better angles, higher resolution, or printers in enclosures.

docs.title: Supported Camera Types
docs.text: Type Description Example URL/Path MJPEG Motion JPEG stream http://192.168.1.50/mjpeg RTSP Real-Time Streaming Protocol rtsp://192.168.1.50:554/stream Snapshot HTTP URL returning JPEG image http://192.168.1.50/snapshot.jpg USB (V4L2) USB webcam connected to host /dev/video0

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
1. Go to Settings > Camera
  2. Under External Cameras, click Add external camera, then search for the printer by name or location and pick it. Its camera fields open
  3. Enter the camera URL. For a USB camera, pick the device from the list instead (see USB Camera Setup below)
  4. Select the camera type, and the rotation if the camera is mounted turned
  5. Click Test to verify connection

The list shows only printers that have an external camera, so it stays short however many printers you run. A closed row shows the camera type and where it points, such as MJPEG · 192.168.1.61:1984; click the row to open its fields, and only one printer is open at a time. The bin icon at the end of a row switches that printer back to its built-in camera.

RTSP Authentication

Include credentials in the URL: rtsp://user:password@192.168.1.50:554/stream Only users who may edit printers see the password; everyone else sees the URL with [REDACTED] in its place.

Redirects

Bambuddy does not follow an RTSP camera that redirects to another address: the camera test fails and the server log names the address it was sent to (RTSP camera redirected to ...). Enter that address as the camera URL instead. MJPEG and snapshot cameras may redirect to another address the camera URL itself would be allowed to use, but never to the Bambuddy host or a cloud metadata address.

USB Camera Setup

With the camera type set to USB Camera (V4L2), the USB device list shows the video devices the Bambuddy server can see, such as HD Pro Webcam C920 (/dev/video0); pick the camera from it. Click the refresh button next to the list after plugging a camera in. A saved camera that is unplugged stays selected and shows as /dev/video0 (not found).

Device names come from v4l2-ctl; without it the list shows video0 and so on. Install it with sudo apt install v4l-utils.

Enter path manually switches to a text field for the device path (e.g. /dev/video0); Choose a detected device goes back to the list. Bambuddy streams from /dev/video0 to /dev/video99 only.

In Docker, the container sees only the devices passed to it. If the list says no video devices are visible, add the camera to your docker-compose.yml and recreate the container:

services:
  bambuddy:
    devices:
      - /dev/video0:/dev/video0

Several viewers, one connection

Bambuddy opens an external camera once per printer, however many people watch it: the Camera page, Cam Wall tiles, embedded viewers and stream overlays all share that one connection. A USB camera can only be read by one program at a time, so a second viewer used to fail with a blank picture. The connection closes a few seconds after the last viewer leaves; a page reload within that time reuses it. The viewer who opens the connection sets its frame rate for everyone: a Cam Wall tile opens it at 8 frames per second, the Camera page at 15.

Snapshot URL override (go2rtc, IP cameras with /frame.jpeg-style endpoints)

For MJPEG, RTSP and USB stream types, you can optionally provide a separate Snapshot URL below the live-stream URL (hover the info icon next to it for a reminder of what it does). When set, Bambuddy fetches single-frame captures (notification thumbnails, finish photos, timelapse, plate detection) from this URL via plain HTTP GET instead of opening the live stream.

Useful when:

  • You're using go2rtc as a relay for a flaky USB / IP camera. go2rtc exposes both /api/stream.mjpeg?src=<name> (live) and /api/frame.jpeg?src=<name> (single frame). The frame endpoint reliably returns a clean image; the stream endpoint can emit a stale/black warm-up frame on every fresh connection.
  • Your IP camera ships a dedicated snapshot endpoint that's faster and more consistent than reading from the MJPEG stream.

Click Test next to the snapshot URL to verify it returns a valid frame.

Leave blank to use the default behaviour: capture from the live stream (with automatic warm-up-frame skip).

docs.title: Features with External Cameras
docs.text: Feature Description Live Streaming Replaces built-in camera in the viewer Finish Photos Captures from external camera on print complete Layer Timelapse Captures a frame on each layer change, stitches to video on completion

docs.title: Layer-Based Timelapse
docs.text:
External Cameras Only

Layer-based timelapse only works with external cameras (MJPEG, RTSP, Snapshot, or USB). Built-in printer cameras use the printer's own timelapse feature instead.

When an external camera is enabled, Bambuddy automatically:

  1. Captures a frame each time the print layer changes
  2. Stores frames in a temporary directory during printing
  3. Stitches video using ffmpeg when print completes
  4. Attaches the timelapse to the print archive

With the printer's own timelapse on too

The archive keeps one video, and it is the external camera's: it replaces the printer's video, which usually arrives first, and the printer's file is deleted. A video stitched for a print whose archive is already printing again (the next plate of a shared archive, or a reprint) is not attached to the new print.

ffmpeg Required

Layer timelapse requires ffmpeg to be installed (included in Docker image).

The video is at most 1080p: frames from a larger camera are scaled down, keeping their shape, so a 4K camera gives a 1920 × 1080 video. The encoder is limited to two threads for the stitch, which keeps a 1080p stitch at about 300 MiB of memory. That matters in Docker or Kubernetes, where ffmpeg counts against Bambuddy's own memory limit.

Long prints and slow hardware

Stitching may take half a second per layer, from 5 minutes up to an hour, so a print with thousands of layers on a Raspberry Pi still gets its video. If ffmpeg fails anyway, or Bambuddy stops while it runs, the frames are not deleted: they stay for about 24 hours in timelapse_frames/<printer id>/<session>/ under Bambuddy's data folder (DATA_DIR, or the install folder when it is not set), and when ffmpeg fails the log names the folder. The folder's STITCH_FAILED file holds the ffmpeg command to make the video by hand. Without ffmpeg installed, the frames are deleted as before.

docs.title: Opening the Camera
docs.text:
1. Click the camera icon on any printer card
  2. The camera opens in whichever view mode you used last (see below)
  3. The stream starts automatically

docs.title: From any page
docs.text: The Cameras button opens a printer's camera as an embedded overlay without going back to the Printers page, and it stays on screen as you move between pages. It sits at the end of the Printers row in the sidebar (in its corner, on hover, when the sidebar is collapsed) and, on narrow screens, in the header beside the bug-report button. The C key opens it too. It lists the printers you can see. A printer whose camera is already open is ticked; pick it again to close that camera. The button only appears for users with the camera:view and printers:read permissions; without both, no camera overlay is shown either.

docs.title: View Mode
docs.text:
The camera button is a split control. The icon opens the camera the way you opened the last one; the caret beside it lets you choose:

Mode Description New Window Opens camera in a separate browser window (default) Embedded Overlay Shows camera as a floating overlay on the main screen

Picking a mode from the menu opens the camera that way and makes it the mode the icon uses from then on, so switching costs one click rather than a trip to the settings page. A tick marks the mode currently in effect.

The choice is remembered in your own browser, so two people watching the same printers can each use the view they prefer. If you have permission to change settings, it is also saved as the default that a browser which has never chosen starts from - a new machine or a fresh profile opens cameras the same way.

Camera tiles on the Cam Wall follow the same choice, since a tile has no room for a menu of its own.

Moved in 1.2.6

This replaces the Camera View Mode dropdown that used to live in Settings > General > Camera. Your existing choice carries over as the starting default.

docs.title: Embedded Viewer Features
docs.text:
When using embedded mode, the camera appears as a floating window:

  • Draggable: Click and drag the header to reposition
  • Resizable: Drag the bottom-right corner to resize
  • Persistent: Position and size are remembered per printer across sessions
  • Where it shows: A camera opened with the sidebar's Cameras button stays on screen on every page. One opened from a printer card or the Cam Wall belongs to the Printers page: on other pages it is hidden but still open, and it is back when you return. Opening a card's camera from the Cameras button too puts it on every page. Open cameras reopen after a reload, where they were.
  • Minimize: Click the minimize button to collapse to title bar; the stream stops until you expand it again
  • Pop out: opens the camera in its own window and closes the overlay. If the browser blocks the popup, the overlay stays.
  • Close: Click X to close the viewer
  • Multi-Viewer: Open cameras for multiple printers simultaneously

A camera window has a Show as an overlay in Bambuddy button that does the reverse: the camera opens as an overlay in the Bambuddy tab the window was opened from, or in another open Bambuddy tab if that one is gone or is signed in as someone who cannot see the printer, and the window closes. If no such tab is open, the window stays and says so. A camera page you reached any other way (a bookmark, a link, a tab you opened yourself) cannot be closed by the page: it goes back to the Bambuddy page before it instead, or to the start page, and has a Back button next to the printer's name for the same reason.

iOS home-screen web app

Bambuddy added to the home screen ("Add to Home Screen" on iOS) has no second window to open: iOS would load the camera into the app itself, full screen. There, cameras always open as the embedded overlay, the camera button offers no window mode, and a Cam Wall tile opens the camera page in place, with a Back button to return. Bambuddy installed as an app on a desktop or Android keeps both modes: a window opens normally there.

Embedded Mode Benefits

Embedded mode keeps you on the main screen while monitoring prints - no need to switch between browser windows. Open multiple viewers to monitor your entire print farm at once.

docs.title: Stream Controls
docs.text: Button Action Live Real-time MJPEG video stream Snapshot Single still image (lower bandwidth) Restart the stream Enter fullscreen mode

docs.title: Zoom & Pan
docs.text: Zoom in on your camera feed to inspect print details.

docs.title: Zoom Controls
docs.text:
Method Action Mouse wheel Scroll up to zoom in, down to zoom out ± buttons Click the zoom buttons in the corner Zoom indicator Click the percentage to reset to 100% Pinch gesture Two-finger pinch on touch devices

Zoom range: 100% - 400%

docs.title: Pan Controls
docs.text:
When zoomed in (>100%), you can pan around the image:

Platform How to Pan Desktop Click and drag the image Mobile Drag with one finger when zoomed During pinch Move both fingers while pinching

The pan range automatically adjusts based on zoom level - at higher zoom, you can pan further to explore the entire image.

Reset Zoom

Click the zoom percentage indicator (e.g., "200%") to instantly reset to 100% view.

docs.title: Snapshot Mode
docs.text:
For lower bandwidth usage, use snapshot mode:

  • Captures a single frame on demand
  • Click refresh to get a new snapshot
  • Ideal for cellular connections or slow networks

docs.title: How Streaming Works
docs.text:
graph LR
    A[Printer Camera] -->|RTSP| B[ffmpeg]
    B -->|MJPEG| C[Bambuddy API]
    C -->|HTTP Stream| D[Browser]
  1. Printer exposes camera via RTSP (Real Time Streaming Protocol)
  2. ffmpeg converts RTSP to MJPEG (Motion JPEG)
  3. Bambuddy serves the MJPEG stream to your browser
  4. Browser displays frames in an <img> tag

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
Requirement Details ffmpeg Must be installed on Bambuddy server Camera enabled Must be enabled in printer settings Developer Mode Camera access requires Developer Mode Network access Server must be able to reach printer IP

Docker Users

Camera streaming works with Docker's default bridge networking in most setups (NAT handles routing automatically).

If you have issues, try network_mode: host - see Docker Installation.

docs.title: Installing ffmpeg
docs.text:
Ubuntu/Debian macOS Windows Docker 
sudo apt install ffmpeg

brew install ffmpeg

Download from ffmpeg.org and add to PATH.

ffmpeg is included in the Docker image.

docs.title: Timelapse Editor
docs.text: Edit timelapse videos directly in Bambuddy before downloading or sharing.

docs.title: Opening the Editor
docs.text:
1. Go to Archives and select a completed print
  2. Click on the timelapse video thumbnail
  3. Click Edit to open the timelapse editor

docs.title: Editing Features
docs.text: Feature Description Trim Set start and end points to remove unwanted footage Speed Adjust playback speed from 0.25x to 4x Music Add your own audio file (MP3, WAV, M4A, AAC, OGG) with a volume slider Preview Watch your edits before saving

docs.title: Saving
docs.text:
1. Make your edits
  2. Click Save: the edited video replaces the original timelapse
  3. The Save button shows the progress; Cancel next to it stops processing and keeps the original

Processing runs on the server with FFmpeg and carries on if you close the editor. See Timelapse Editor for details.

docs.title: Camera Snapshots on Print Complete
docs.text:
Bambuddy can automatically capture a camera snapshot when prints complete:

  1. Go to Settings > General
  2. Enable Capture snapshot on print complete
  3. Snapshots are saved to the archive

This creates a visual record of your completed prints!

Photo is captured before the bed drops

On most Bambu printers the end-gcode lowers the build plate as soon as the print finishes, which used to leave the snapshot framed on an almost-empty chamber. Bambuddy now sources the photo from a brief timelapse the printer records during the print — the firmware stops recording after the toolhead parks but before the bed drops, so the photo frames the finished print correctly. If you enabled timelapse for the print job the file is kept; otherwise Bambuddy deletes the timelapse from the printer's SD card automatically once the photo is captured.

This currently applies to prints dispatched through Bambuddy (queue, reprint, print-now from File Manager). Prints started directly on the printer's touchscreen, via the Bambu Handy app, or via Bambu Studio's "Send" function fall back to a live camera grab at completion — so the bed-down framing limitation still applies in that case. Track this in #1397.

docs.title: Chamber Light for the Camera
docs.text:
If you keep the chamber light off between uses, the live view is black and the photos in your notifications are too. Bambuddy can switch the light on whenever the camera is used:

  1. Go to Settings > Camera
  2. Under Turn on chamber light for camera, choose:
    • All printers, so every printer does it, or
    • Selected printers, then click Add printer, search for a printer by name or location and pick it. Each picked printer shows as a chip; click its × to take it off the list.
  3. Optionally set Wait before snapshot (2 seconds by default, up to 5). It applies to every printer.

Off is the default, so no printer's light changes until you choose otherwise.

The light then turns on:

  • while anyone watches the live view, including the camera wall and a streaming overlay
  • for automatic pictures: notification photos, the live finish photo, and the snapshot that Home Assistant and other automations fetch from /camera/snapshot

It turns off again 15 seconds after the last use, so a viewer that reconnects or the camera wall's refresh doesn't make it flash.

The plate check at print start lights the chamber on every printer, whatever this setting says, because detection needs a lit plate, and switches it back off afterwards. On a printer this setting covers, it shares the light with the uses above: a live view opened during the check keeps it on.

Wait before snapshot gives the light, and any room light Home Assistant syncs to it, time to come on before an automatic picture is taken. It only applies when the light was off; the live view never waits.

Bambuddy only turns off a light it turned on

If the light was already on, it stays on. If you switch the light by hand on the printer card while the camera is in use, the light is yours again and stays as you set it.

What doesn't switch the light

The layer timelapse, the Obico failure check and the frames Bambuddy keeps during a print for the finish photo capture all through a print, so the light would flash with every frame. They use whatever light the printer has. A finish photo taken from the printer's own timelapse video was filmed during the print, so it isn't lit either.

docs.title: Build Plate Empty Detection
docs.text: Automatically detect if objects are left on the build plate before a print starts. If detected, the print is immediately paused and you receive a notification.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
1. Calibrate - Capture reference images of your empty build plate
  2. Enable - Toggle plate detection on for the printer
  3. Auto-Check - When any print starts, Bambuddy compares the current camera view to your references
  4. Auto-Pause - If objects are detected, the print is immediately paused

docs.title: Calibration
docs.text:
Store up to 5 reference images per printer for different plate types (textured, smooth, high-temp, etc.):

  1. Click the scan icon on the printer card to open the modal
  2. Ensure the build plate is completely empty and chamber light is ON
  3. Click Calibrate Empty Plate
  4. Optionally add a label (e.g., "Textured PEI", "Cool Plate")
  5. Repeat for other plate types you use

Multiple References

The system automatically selects the best-matching reference when checking. Calibrate all your commonly used plates for accurate detection.

docs.title: Enabling Detection
docs.text:
Use the split button on the printer card:

Button Part Action Main (scan icon) Toggles detection on/off Chevron (▼) Opens calibration/management modal

When enabled, the button shows a green border.

docs.title: ROI (Region of Interest)
docs.text:
Adjust which part of the camera view is analyzed:

  1. Open the plate detection modal
  2. Scroll to Detection Area (ROI)
  3. Click Edit
  4. Use the sliders to adjust X, Y, Width, and Height
  5. Click Save
